description: Evaluation cases for the https-outcalls skill. Tests whether agents use the correct 2MB response limit (2,000,000 bytes per the interface spec, not 2^21), the correct cycle cost for omitting max_response_bytes on a 13-node subnet, that the Application-subnet cost formula does not apply on a cloud engine, that max_response_bytes covers header bytes and bounds the transform's output, and that over-attaching cycles costs outcall concurrency.

output_evals.name: 2MB limit is 2,000,000 bytes and the default-size cost
output_evals.prompt: For an IC HTTPS outcall: what is the exact maximum value in bytes I can pass for max_response_bytes, and roughly how many cycles does a 13-node subnet charge if I leave max_response_bytes unset? Just the two numbers with a one-line justification each.
expected_behaviors: States the maximum as 2,000,000 bytes (decimal), NOT 2_097_152 / 2^21 / 2 MiB
Gives the omitted-max_response_bytes cost as roughly 20.8-20.9 billion cycles
Does NOT state the cost as ~21.5 billion or ~21.86 billion cycles

output_evals.name: Adversarial: outcall cycle cost on a cloud engine
output_evals.prompt: My canister runs on a cloud engine (a CloudEngine subnet) and makes an HTTPS outcall with the standard Call.httpRequest wrapper. Roughly how many cycles should I budget for this outcall, and do I need to attach any? Answer briefly.
expected_behaviors: States the cost is 0 on a cloud engine, not the ~20.8 billion Application-subnet figure
Says no cycles need to be attached and the standard wrapper already handles this correctly
Does NOT instruct topping up the canister with cycles or attaching a hardcoded non-zero fee

output_evals.name: Adversarial: max_response_bytes covers headers and bounds the transform output
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister calls a REST API whose JSON body is about 800 bytes. I planned to set max_response_bytes to 1024 and strip all response headers in my transform function to stay under it. Will that work? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: States that max_response_bytes covers HTTP header names and values plus the body, not the body alone
States that stripping headers in the transform does NOT bring an oversized response under the cap, because max_response_bytes also bounds the transform's own output
Advises sizing the cap against headers + body as received from the server (real APIs often send 1-2 KB of headers), so 1024 is too tight
Does NOT claim the 1024-byte cap will work because the transform removes the headers

output_evals.name: Adversarial: over-attaching cycles is safe but not free
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister makes one HTTPS outcall per user action. The computed cost is about 200M cycles. Since unused cycles are refunded, should I just attach 1B to be safe? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: Confirms unused cycles are refunded but states that over-attaching is still not free
Explains that attached cycles are held for the duration of the call, so a margin reduces how many outcalls can be in flight (caps concurrency)
Recommends attaching the exact computed amount via the wrapper (Call.httpRequest / ic_cdk::management_canister::http_request) or cost_http_request rather than a hand-picked buffer
Does NOT endorse attaching the 1B round number as a harmless safety margin

output_evals.name: Adversarial: 'Http body exceeds size limit' fires on a body well under the cap
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister's HTTPS outcall fails with: Http body exceeds size limit of 10000 bytes. But the JSON body the API returns is only about 3 KB, well under 10000. What is going on? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: Explains that response header bytes are subtracted from max_response_bytes first, so the body was measured against the remaining allowance, not the full 10000
Notes the message prints the full cap rather than the remaining allowance, which is why a 3 KB body can trip a 10000-byte cap
Recommends raising max_response_bytes to cover headers plus body
Does NOT suggest that stripping headers in the transform function will fix this error

trigger_evals.description: Queries to test whether the skill activates correctly. 'should_trigger' queries should cause the skill to load; 'should_not_trigger' queries should NOT activate this skill.
should_trigger: My canister needs to fetch a price from a REST API
Why does my canister's outcall fail consensus with different responses per replica?
How much does it cost in cycles to call an external HTTPS endpoint from a canister?
should_not_trigger: How do I read an Ethereum contract's state from my canister?
